Vision · Month 2 experiment

GuideCane Lite

Two strong sensors on an existing metal cane.

This is a $28.95 electronics retrofit for an existing hollow aluminium cane and an existing USB power bank. It is not the cost of a newly purchased, complete cane. One VL53L1X faces forward for obstacles; a second sits in a guarded pod just above the tip and looks down and slightly ahead for a possible drop. The wires pass through the reused metal tube.

What remains

SenseForward obstacle + near-tip ground distance
→
DecidePico 2 checks two separate I²C buses
→
AlertDifferent beeps for obstacle and possible drop

The raised button requests a forward distance check. A long press cycles three alert-volume levels in software. The cane cannot identify whether the return is a person, wall or vehicle. With no rear-facing sensor, it does not repeatedly detect the holder's legs.

What was removed

The eight-direction ring, seven extra ToF modules, multiplexer, new tube purchase, new battery and charger, vibration motor, grip pressure sensor, hook fabrication and printed enclosures are outside this $30 retrofit. The existing tactile cane tip remains in use.

12 mm tactile scan button$0.75

New-parts subtotal$28.95

Required reused items: a suitable hollow metal cane with tactile tip, a 5 V USB power bank and cable, and secure mounts made from available materials. If these must be bought, the project exceeds $30. A new 4 ft aluminium tube alone is $16.62, raising this subtotal to at least $45.57 before tip, battery, mounting and shipping. The $5.97 ST part is a bare chip and needs a custom PCB; it does not replace the $8.95 ready-to-wire module in this prototype.

Weight and limits
Two M5Stack modules weigh about 8.6 g total. Added electronics and wiring are estimated at roughly 25–45 g before the reused power bank and mounts. Final mass depends on the chosen cane. One forward beam does not cover the whole walking path; one downward beam can miss narrow holes and can fail on difficult surfaces. The tip and normal cane technique remain essential. Treat this as a supervised experiment, not a tested mobility aid.

Real component photos
